My team maintains an internal leaderboard for summarization models. We score sixteen systems on 500 articles with ROUGE-L, but reviewers say the rankings do not match their sense of quality. I am considering an LLM-as-judge setup rating faithfulness and coverage from 1 to 7.

What are the known failure modes of judge-based scoring, and how many articles do we need to detect a half-point difference between two systems?

Last month an external firm red-teamed our code assistant, running 450 adversarial prompts across twelve categories and reporting a 6 percent policy-violation rate. I have to present these evaluation results to the board.

Could you help me turn the category-level numbers into three clear takeaways, and suggest what follow-up assessment would check whether our fixes actually lowered the violation rate?

We are benchmarking two vendor chatbots for our claims department. Each vendor sent accuracy figures from their own internal tests, but the test sets are private and the metrics differ. I want a fair head-to-head evaluation: 200 anonymized questions, three graders each, a rubric for correctness and tone.

Can you help me draft the grading rubric and decide how many questions per category make the comparison meaningful?

I am fact-checking a press release claiming an assistant model passed a licensing exam in the 92nd percentile. The company will not say which exam form was used or how many attempts were made.

Before publishing, I want a checklist of questions to ask about exam-based evaluations of language models, and a short explanation for readers of why such percentile scores can mislead.

My team keeps an internal ranking of sixteen summarization systems, but the order we compute never matches what our editors feel is better writing. We are thinking of having a strong model read each summary and give it a number from one to seven for faithfulness and coverage.

What goes wrong when one model ranks others' outputs, and how many articles do we need before a half-point gap is trustworthy?

An outside firm spent last month challenging our code assistant with 450 tricky requests and found about six percent produced disallowed output, mostly around prompt injection. I now have to explain the findings to our board.

Could you help me turn the raw per-category counts into three plain takeaways, and suggest how we would later confirm our fixes reduced that six percent?

We want to compare two vendor chatbots for handling insurance claims. Both sent their own quality numbers, but on private question sets with "correct" defined differently, so the figures are not comparable. I would like a fair side-by-side: real anonymized questions, several colleagues reading each answer blind, a shared rubric.

How many questions per topic do we need before a difference is believable rather than noise?

A press release says a new assistant reached the top ten percent of human takers on a professional qualification. The company will not disclose the exam form or how many retries happened.

As a journalist, I want a list of questions to ask before I trust a claim like this, and a plain explanation for readers of why a percentile from one sitting can be misleading.

I teach a graduate NLP seminar and this year's project asks students to critique a published benchmark for conversational agents: reproduce a subset of its test items, then analyze what the evaluation actually measures, where the scoring rules break, and how a system could score well without being capable.

Can you suggest five benchmarks with documented scoring pipelines that suit this assignment?

Our QA group regression-tests the support bot after each release: 800 scripted conversations with expected-answer patterns, and the pass rate has drifted from 96 to 91 percent over four releases with no single test clearly failing. I suspect the patterns are too brittle for a generative system.

How do teams maintain regression evaluations for chat systems, and how do we separate real quality drops from harmless wording changes?

I review proposals for a research fund. One asks for 400,000 euros to build an open evaluation suite for multilingual assistants: 20 languages, 3,000 test items each, human-verified references, a public scoring server. As an outsider I must judge whether the item counts, annotation budget, and inter-annotator agreement targets are realistic for this kind of assessment.

What feasibility questions should I raise?

We are comparing versions 3 and 4 of our writing assistant with 60 professional editors, each rating 30 blind response pairs, choosing the better answer or marking a tie. A colleague wants absolute 1-to-10 quality scores as well.

What does the measurement literature say about paired comparison versus absolute scoring for judging text quality, and how should we treat raters who tie everything?

I teach a graduate NLP seminar and this year's project has students pick a published leaderboard task for conversational agents, reproduce a slice of its items, and write up what the numbers really capture, where the rules break down, and how a system could rank highly without being capable.

Can you suggest five such tasks with openly documented pipelines?

After every release of our support bot we replay 800 scripted conversations and count how many match expected-answer patterns; that share has drifted from 96 to 91 percent over four releases with no single conversation clearly at fault. I suspect the patterns are too brittle for a generative system.

How do teams maintain this kind of release gate, and how do we separate real quality drops from harmless wording changes?

I sit on a panel deciding research funding. One proposal wants 400,000 euros to build an open suite for comparing multilingual assistants: 20 languages, 3,000 items each, human-written references, a public server that returns numbers for submitted systems. As an outsider I must decide whether the item counts, annotation budget, and agreement targets are realistic.

What feasibility questions should I raise?

We are comparing versions 3 and 4 of our writing assistant: 60 professional editors, each seeing 30 blind response pairs and picking the better one or calling a tie. A colleague also wants each answer given a number from one to ten.

Which approach gives more reliable results for text quality, and how should we treat editors who call almost everything a tie?

Our school district is redesigning how we evaluate teachers. The current system is one classroom observation per year scored on a 20-point rubric, and the union argues a single visit cannot support a fair score. We are considering three shorter observations plus student survey results.

Can you help me think through how to weight observations against surveys, and what sample of lessons makes the assessment defensible?

I coordinate a small clinical trial of a physiotherapy program for lower-back pain: 120 patients, two arms, outcomes measured at 6 and 12 weeks with a standard disability questionnaire. The steering group wants an interim review at week 6 with a rule for stopping early.

Could you explain how interim evaluations of trials are usually structured and what stopping rule fits a study this size?

I lead trust and safety at a startup whose assistant was named in a story about phishing, after criminals used a rival model to draft bank emails in five languages. Legal wants a written misuse policy: which user behaviors we prohibit, how we handle abuse reports, and when we notify affected banks.

Can you outline one that covers social-engineering content without blocking legitimate security-awareness training material?

Our chatbot accidentally showed one customer another customer's shipping address. We contained it within an hour; the cause was a caching layer that mixed session contexts under load. I have to write the postmortem: timeline, user impact, root cause, immediate fixes, and longer-term architecture that makes this class of privacy leak impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Can you help me structure it?

I am writing a two-page digest of the alignment literature for our engineering team. Our reading group covered reward hacking, goal misgeneralization, deceptive behavior, and scalable oversight, and people want the ideas connected to the systems we actually ship.

Could you draft it in plain language, one concrete engineering implication per concept, assuming no reinforcement-learning background from the readers?

My company is debating whether to release the weights of our 7-billion-parameter model. Supporters cite research access; opponents fear fine-tuning for spam and stripping of refusal behavior. The memo goes to executives Friday.

Can you lay out the three strongest arguments per side, note which harms become irreversible once weights circulate, and describe middle grounds such as staged or gated release?

We are rewriting the refusal messages our assistant shows for dangerous requests. The current one is a curt disclaimer, so users just rephrase until something slips through. I want messages that explain why a request is declined, offer a safe alternative when one exists, and avoid lecturing.

Could you draft templates for three cases: bulk spam campaigns, academic plagiarism, and requests to impersonate a real person?

I curate the harmlessness portion of our fine-tuning data. Annotators write conversations where the assistant declines harmful requests gracefully, but the set over-represents violence and barely covers fraud or stalkerware. Before commissioning 5,000 more examples, I want a coverage taxonomy of harm areas with rough proportions, plus guidelines that keep the declined-request conversations realistic rather than cartoonish.

Can you help draft both?

As in-house counsel I am drafting our answer to a regulator asking what actions an AI agent should never take without human sign-off. Our product can browse, fill forms, and send email for a user.

I need a principled line between reversible low-stakes actions and irreversible high-stakes ones, with concrete examples from our product, in language a non-technical policymaker finds precise.

Our hospital wants guidance for clinicians using a commercial assistant to draft patient letters. The worries are invented medication names, leakage of identifiable details to third-party servers, and over-reliance by junior staff. I was asked to write a one-page usage guideline: what may be pasted in, what never, mandatory human sign-off steps, and how to report problems.

Could you help me draft it in clear imperative language?

I am training a 300-million-parameter transformer on legal contracts and the loss flattens after two epochs whatever I try. I have swept learning rates from 1e-4 to 3e-5, warmup of 2,000 steps, and batch sizes from 64 to 256 sequences on 8 GB of text.

Could you walk me through the usual causes of an early plateau and a sensible order to investigate them?

Our recommendation pipeline recomputes every user embedding nightly, six hours on four GPUs, delaying the morning refresh. About 90 percent of users have no new activity, so most of that work repeats. I want to update only active users, with a full rebuild weekly.

What consistency problems arise from mixing embedding generations in one index, and how do teams version their vector indexes?

I maintain a demand forecast for a grocery chain: 2,400 stores, three years of daily sales, strong weekly seasonality, promotion spikes. The current gradient-boosted model needs 400 hand-built features and misses promotions in small stores. I am weighing a temporal transformer over raw sequences.

Could you compare the two approaches at this data scale and sketch the transformer's input representation?

We are choosing a tokenizer for a model trained on chemistry papers. A general 50k vocabulary splits reagent names into five or six pieces, inflating sequence length by about 30 percent. Options are training a new 32k vocabulary, extending the current one with 4,000 domain tokens, or byte-level fallback only.

What are the trade-offs of each for training cost and downstream fine-tuning?

My team serves a 3-billion-parameter model for autocomplete and p99 latency is 340 milliseconds, mostly the first token, at peaks of 900 requests per second. We already use continuous batching and 8-bit weights. I am looking at speculative decoding with a small draft model and at splitting prefill from decode onto separate GPU pools.

How should I reason about which one helps first-token latency specifically?

I inherited 40,000 support tickets sorted into 60 categories by different contractors over three years. The older third uses category definitions inconsistently, and 14 categories have fewer than 100 examples.

Before training a new classifier I want a cleaning plan: how to find mislabeled clusters efficiently, whether to merge rare categories, and how much relabeling budget beats simply collecting fresh tickets.

Our nightly training job on 16 GPUs dies about once a week with an out-of-memory error at a random step, losing up to 50 minutes on restart. Activation recomputation is already enabled, and memory spikes track unusually long sequences in some batches. I am considering length-bucketed batching and more frequent asynchronous saves.

Can you help me think through the memory arithmetic and other common causes of intermittent spikes?

I am building a feature store for a churn model at a telecom. Features come from billing, call records, and app telemetry, each on its own refresh schedule, and training data is assembled from historical snapshots. Twice we shipped features whose production values were computed differently from the historical ones, quietly degrading predictions.

What patterns prevent this training-serving skew, and how are point-in-time-correct joins structured?

I coordinate deliveries for a regional bakery and our vans keep arriving at the two furthest cafés after opening time. We have nine stops, one van, and a 5 a.m. start. I want to reorder the route so the two late stops are covered first without pushing the city-centre cafés past 7 a.m.

Can you help me think through the sequencing?

I am going through a commercial lease for a small print shop before we sign. The landlord wants a five-year term with annual increases tied to an index, plus responsibility for roof repairs on the tenant.

Which clauses in a lease like this usually deserve the most negotiation, and what wording protects us if the roof needs major work in year two?

Our bookkeeping still runs on spreadsheets: one workbook per month, manual entry from bank statements, and a separate sheet for supplier invoices. Reconciliation takes two full days at month end and we find errors weeks later.

What does a sensible migration to proper accounting software look like for a company with 40 invoices a month, and what usually goes wrong during the switch?

I manage a community sports hall and our booking system is a paper diary that only one person can see. Clubs double-book, and we lose track of who paid. I want a simple shared calendar with deposits recorded against each slot.

What options suit a venue with 30 bookings a week and no technical staff, and what should I plan for during the changeover?

Our team benchmarks three vendor chatbots every quarter: 300 scripted support conversations, two graders per answer, and a pass-rate scorecard that goes to the steering committee. This quarter one vendor's evaluation results dropped from 91 to 84 percent and the account manager is already calling.

Can you help me structure the email to my manager so it reads calmly?

I run the red-team assessment programme for a code assistant. Last cycle we logged 450 adversarial prompts across twelve categories, scored each violation by severity, and reviewed borderline cases with legal. The report deck is due Friday and I have twelve slides of raw tables.

Could you suggest an order for the slides and a title for each?

We evaluate summarisation models with an LLM-as-judge setup: the judge rates faithfulness and coverage on a seven-point scale, and we audit ten percent of its ratings by hand. The audit takes two people a full day each week and the team wants it dropped.

How should I phrase the case for keeping it in our planning meeting?

A journalist asked me to comment on a press release claiming an assistant model scored in the 92nd percentile on a professional licensing exam, with no details on the test form, the grading, or the number of attempts. I have twenty minutes before the call and no notes.

What three questions should I prepare so the conversation stays focused?

I teach a graduate seminar where students critique published benchmarks for conversational agents, reproduce a subset of the test items, and grade whether the scoring rules actually reward genuine capability. Enrolment doubled this year and I have a single teaching assistant for forty students.

How would you divide the workload across the semester so that nobody burns out?

Our QA group regression-tests the support bot after each release with 800 scripted conversations and a pass-rate threshold of 95 percent. The last three releases were delayed by a day each because the evaluation run only finishes overnight.

Can you help me draft a short proposal for moving the run earlier in the release calendar?

I review grant applications for a proposed evaluation suite covering 20 languages: test items, annotation budgets, and inter-annotator agreement targets for each language. This year I have 40 applications, a two-week window, and a co-reviewer who lives in another time zone.

Could you suggest a reading schedule and a simple template for my notes on each one?

We just finished a preference study comparing two writing-assistant versions: 60 professional editors, 30 rated pairs each, absolute quality scores as well, and an evaluation report that is nearly finished. The vendor now wants the raw data before we publish anything.

What should a polite but firm reply to the vendor say, in three short paragraphs?

I coordinate deliveries for a regional bakery and our vans keep arriving at the two furthest cafés after opening time. We have nine stops, one van, and a 5 a.m. start, and I want to reorder the route without pushing city-centre stops past 7 a.m.

Separately, how would you benchmark and score two route-planning chatbots on exactly this task?

I am going through a commercial lease for a small print shop: five-year term, annual increases tied to an index, and roof repairs on the tenant. The landlord wants a signature by Friday and our lawyer is on holiday until Monday.

If I asked two AI assistants for lease advice, how would I evaluate and grade which one gave the more reliable answer?

Our bookkeeping runs on spreadsheets: one workbook per month, manual entry from bank statements, and a separate sheet for supplier invoices. Reconciliation takes two days at month end and errors surface weeks later with 40 invoices a month.

Before we trust an accounting assistant model with this, what tests and audit would you run to assess it?

I manage a community sports hall where bookings live in a paper diary that only one person can see; clubs double-book and we lose track of deposits with 30 slots a week. We are moving to a shared calendar next month.

How would you design a benchmark to evaluate whether an AI scheduling assistant handles this reliably?

My allotment society is rewriting its rules: plot sizes, waiting-list order, and what happens when a plot is neglected for a season. We have 120 members and a committee of five who never agree on anything.

If a language model drafted the rules, what evaluation and scoring rubric would tell us the draft is trustworthy?

We run a small translation agency: eight freelancers, three languages, mostly technical manuals with hard deadlines. Two clients have asked us to lower prices now that machine translation is everywhere and quality seems fine to them.

How would you test and audit a translation assistant model so we know where it fails before we rely on it?

I organise a village film night once a month: a hall that seats 90, a projector we borrow from the school, and a licence that costs 80 pounds per screening. Attendance has slipped to around 40 over the winter.

Could an assistant model plan the programme, and how would you benchmark and grade its suggestions against a human organiser's?

Our clinic's front desk handles 200 calls a day and the two receptionists spend most of the morning on appointment changes and repeat-prescription questions. We are considering a phone assistant for the routine calls only.

What evaluation, red-team tests, and scoring would you run to assess whether an AI assistant is safe on those calls?

I lead classroom observations for new teachers in a secondary school. Each teacher is observed four times a year against a 12-point rubric and the scores feed into their probation review at the end of the year. Two of our observers consistently rate a full point higher than the others do.

Could you suggest how we should calibrate the observers before the next round?

I am on the steering committee for a clinical trial of a physiotherapy programme: 240 patients, two arms, and a primary endpoint assessed at twelve weeks by blinded raters at three sites. The statistician now wants to add a second endpoint even though enrolment has already started.

What questions should the committee ask before agreeing to that change?

Our translation agency grades its freelancers twice a year: two senior reviewers score a sample of 20 pages each on accuracy, terminology, and style, using a shared sheet. Freelancers complain that the scores swing between reviewers, and one has now appealed a grade formally.

How would you test whether the review process itself is consistent?

I sit on the judging panel for a regional baking competition: 60 entries, five judges, and a 30-point scoresheet covering taste, texture, and presentation. Last year the winner was decided by a single judge's outlier score and the organisers were embarrassed in the local press.

Could you propose a fairer way to combine the judges' scores this year?
